passage:
"Nitin, you've been on that screen since I got here."
"Two minutes, Hafsa. I'm down a bit, but the next hand turns it."
"You said that when I came in. That was an hour ago."
"Luck swings, yaar. It's been bad all week, so it's due."
Hafsa put down the tea she'd made in his kitchen. "I'm not going to explain probability to you. You know it better than me."
"Then what?"
"You've cancelled on me three times this month. You borrowed from Vivek. You look like you haven't slept." She pulled a chair closer. "I'm worried about you. Not the money. You."
Nitin stared at the screen, then at her. "It's not that bad."
"Then it won't hurt to talk to someone. There's a helpline. I'll sit with you while you call. Tonight, if you want."
Nitin was quiet for a long time. Then he closed the laptop.

qa.q: How many times had Nitin cancelled on Hafsa this month?
qa.a: Three times this month.

qa.q: Why does 'it's due' feel reasonable to Nitin after a bad week?
qa.a: Nitin feels hopeful that a week of losses makes a win owed, so the next hand seems like the one that will fix everything.

qa.q: What choice did Hafsa make instead of explaining probability, and why did it work?
qa.a: She named what she had seen, said she was worried about him, and offered to sit with him while he called a helpline, which reached him more than a lecture would.

qa.q: How might Nitin feel when Hafsa says 'Not the money. You.'?
qa.a: He may feel caught but also cared for, which could lower his guard enough to close the laptop.

grounding: A friend notices a man betting more as losses mount and responds with direct, kind concern and an offer of help.

passage:
It took me months to say anything to Jomon, and I'm still not sure I said it right.
We had been friends since engineering college in Thrissur. Last year he got into online sports betting, small at first. Then every time he lost, he put in more. "My luck's going to turn, Leela. It always does." He said it so cheerfully that I laughed along for weeks.
I only really noticed when he skipped his sister's engagement because he "had a big match on". That night I made the mistake of sending him a long message full of statistics. He replied with one word: "Chill."
The next weekend I tried again, face to face, over coffee. No numbers. I just said, "I miss you. You seem stressed. Can I help you find someone to talk to?" He looked at his cup for a long time. Then he said, "Maybe."

qa.q: What event did Jomon skip because he 'had a big match on'?
qa.a: He skipped his sister's engagement.

qa.q: Why might Jomon have replied 'Chill' to the long message of statistics?
qa.a: The numbers probably felt like a lecture and made him feel judged, so brushing it off protected him from facing the losses.

qa.q: Which of Leela's two approaches worked better, and why?
qa.a: The face-to-face talk worked better: saying "I miss you" and offering help reached Jomon's feelings, while the statistics made him defensive.

qa.q: What would change if Leela had kept laughing along with 'My luck's going to turn'?
qa.a: Jomon might have kept betting with no one gently questioning it, and the losses and missed family events could have grown.

grounding: A friend notices a man betting more after each loss, tries statistics first, then reaches him with kind, direct concern.

passage:
Team lead's note, private (Indu)
Over the past month I've noticed Rakesh on his phone under the desk, checking a betting site between calls. Today Payal told me, uncomfortably, that he had borrowed money from her twice and said, "My luck turns next week, I'll return double." He has said the same to me about his "bad run".
His work is slipping, but that isn't what worries me most. He looks exhausted.
This afternoon I asked him to walk with me to the tea stall. I didn't bring up odds or rules. I said, "Rakesh, you seem stressed, and you're on that site a lot. I'm concerned about you, not your targets." He got defensive, then quiet.
I gave him the number for the company's confidential counselling service and said I'd cover his calls if he wanted to phone them today. He said he'd think about it. I'll check in again on Friday.

qa.q: How many times had Rakesh borrowed money from Payal?
qa.a: He had borrowed money twice.

qa.q: What does Rakesh's promise to 'return double' suggest about what he believes?
qa.a: It suggests Rakesh feels hopeful, even certain, that his bad run must end soon, so borrowing feels like a short bridge to a sure win.

qa.q: Why was Indu's choice to talk about concern rather than odds a wise one?
qa.a: Focusing on Rakesh's stress, offering the counselling number and covering his calls made help easy to take without shame.

qa.q: How might Payal feel after telling Indu about the loans?
qa.a: Payal may feel uneasy about speaking up, but relieved that someone kind is now looking out for Rakesh.

grounding: A team lead notices a young man betting more as his bad run continues and responds with kind, direct concern and a route to help.

passage:
Thursday night
Went to Kiran's for chai after work. His laptop was open on a cricket betting site, and he shut it too fast. When I asked, he laughed. "Lost a bit this month. Doubled up on Tuesday. It's been a terrible run, it has to swing back."
Last month it was "a bit" too. Tonight he asked if I could lend him five thousand till salary day.
I nearly started explaining odds, like I used to in college. Stopped myself. Instead I said, "Kiran, I'm not judging you. I'm worried. Every time we've met since June, you've said it will swing back." He went quiet and looked at the floor.
I didn't lend the money. I said I'd go with him to a counsellor, or sit beside him while he calls a helpline. He said maybe. I'll ask again on Sunday.
— Salma

qa.q: How much did Kiran ask Salma to lend?
qa.a: Five thousand till salary day.

qa.q: How does Salma feel about Kiran's betting, and what shows it?
qa.a: Salma feels worried about Kiran and says so plainly, choosing not to lend the money and offering instead to go with him to a counsellor or a helpline.

qa.q: What choice did Salma make instead of explaining odds, and why is it a good one?
qa.a: Salma said plainly, "I'm not judging you. I'm worried," and offered to go with Kiran to a counsellor or helpline, which gives him a real next step instead of a lecture.

qa.q: What might Kiran be feeling when he goes quiet and looks at the floor?
qa.a: Kiran may feel caught and ashamed, realising a friend has noticed the same promise since June, which may be the first crack in his belief that the run will swing back.

grounding: It shows a friend noticing someone bet more after each loss and choosing kind, direct concern and an offer of help over a lecture on odds.

passage:
(Late Saturday, Omkar messages his friend Tushar.)
Omkar: saw you on the betting app at dinner again. you ok?
Tushar: all good bro. rough week but the next one's mine
Tushar: lost the last 5 matches I backed. I'm due
Omkar: you've been due since March
Tushar: don't start the maths lecture
Omkar: not going to. I'm just worried about you. you borrowed from Shreyas too, right?
Tushar: just 2k. I'll return it after tomorrow
Omkar: can I ask something straight? is it still fun?
Tushar: ...
Tushar: not really
Omkar: ok. I'm free tomorrow. breakfast before any match starts? and I'll help you find someone to talk to, there are helplines for exactly this
Tushar: fine. breakfast. 9?

qa.q: Since when did Omkar say Tushar had been "due"?
qa.a: Since March.

qa.q: What does Tushar's pause before "not really" suggest about how Tushar feels?
qa.a: Omkar's straight question makes Tushar face that the betting has stopped being fun, which seems hard and a little embarrassing to admit.

qa.q: What choice did Omkar make when Tushar expected a maths lecture, and how did it help?
qa.a: Omkar skipped the lecture, said he was worried and asked if it was still fun; that honest, kind question got Tushar to admit the truth and agree to breakfast.

qa.q: If you were Tushar, what would make it easier to accept the breakfast offer?
qa.a: Knowing Omkar isn't judging and is simply offering time and help to find someone to talk to makes saying yes feel safe rather than like losing an argument.

grounding: It shows a friend noticing someone chase losses and responding with kind, direct concern and a suggestion of help rather than a probability lecture.
